title: Portable-size artificial uterine system for viviparous shark embryos
author: Tomita, Kaneko, et al.
materials: DRI-CHEM NX600 automated clinical chemistry analyzer

A single pregnant slender lanternshark (Etmopterus molleri) was obtained from local fishermen at a depth of approximately 500 m, off the main island of Okinawa on December 8th, 2023. Fish were captured using hook-and-line fishing and maintained in a cooler box filled with seawater in a fishing boat. This specimen died during the 6-h return trip and was donated to the Okinawa Churaumi Aquarium (Okinawa, Japan) on the same day of capture. In the aquarium, we dissected the specimen and recovered six embryos from the uterus. Immediately after dissection, the embryos were introduced into an artificial uterus. The condition of the embryo in the artificial uterus was visually assessed twice a day (9:00 and 17:00) by observing respiratory behavior (e.g., movement of gill flaps and spiracular valve) and response to light stimuli (e.g., body undulation and changing body posture). The fluid temperature was maintained at 12 °C throughout the incubation period, which was close to that of the natural habitat of the species.

The embryos were maintained in the artificial uterine fluid, which was developed as described in a previous study [2]. This fluid was prepared by dissolving 3.5 kg of urea in 46 L of chlorine-free tap water, which was made up to a final volume of 100 L using filtered seawater. Through incubation, the chemical composition of the fluid gradually shifted away from that of the artificial uterine fluid and into full-strength seawater in a stepwise manner. This allowed the embryo to acclimate to the seawater environment. During this acclimation process, the incubation fluid was prepared by mixing artificial uterine fluid and seawater while changing the mixing ratio following the protocol developed in a previous study [3]: 100/0, 75/25, 50/50, 25/75, 12.5/87.5, and 6.3/93.7. The interval between each step of chemical composition shift was approximately one week.

The chemical composition of the incubation fluid was monitored every two–four days for sodium and urea and daily for ammonia using a DRI-CHEM NX600 automated clinical chemistry analyzer (Fujifilm Co., Tokyo, Japan). Because the ammonia concentration increased through time, the incubation fluid was replaced with new fluid trying to keep the ammonia concentration under 200 µg/dL. Fluid replacement for each embryo was conducted as follows: first, the embryo in the incubation container was moved to a clean container filled with fresh incubation fluid (Fig. 2A). Second, an additional 2 L of fresh incubation fluid was poured into the container to wash the body surface of the embryo (Fig. 2B). Third, the container with the embryo was placed in a clean 8-L aquarium filled with fresh incubation fluid and returned to the refrigerator (Fig. 2C). The used aquarium and container were washed with 0.1 % sodium hypochlorite solution, rinsed with tap water, dried, and used in the next fluid replacement.Fig. 2Protocol for fluid replacement. A. steps.title: Assemble artificial uterine system
steps.instruction: Place two 8‑L cubic glass aquariums inside a mini‑size refrigerator (R4G‑63SLB, internal volume 63 L) for temperature control. Fill each aquarium with 5 L incubation fluid. Position a cylindrical glass container (13 cm diameter, 6.5 cm height) on the aquarium floor, cover its top with a silicone‑rubber net (5 mm mesh) to allow fluid exchange, and place a single embryo in each container. Supply air near the bottom of each aquarium (outside the container). Keep the entire system in darkness; for observation, install LED lights inside the refrigerator and cover them with red plastic film to minimize light stress.

substeps.instruction: Place two 8‑L glass aquariums in the refrigerator.
Add 5 L incubation fluid to each aquarium.
Put a 13 cm × 6.5 cm glass cylinder on the floor of each aquarium.
Cover cylinder top with a 5 mm‑mesh silicone rubber net.
Insert one embryo per cylinder.
Supply air near the aquarium bottom, outside the cylinder.
Maintain darkness; use LED lights with red film for occasional observation.

steps.title: Collect and place embryos
steps.instruction: Obtain a pregnant slender lanternshark (Etmopterus molleri) from local fishermen (≈500 m depth, Okinawa, 8 Dec 2023). After capture, keep the fish in a cooler box with seawater on the boat; the specimen died during the 6‑h return trip and was donated to the aquarium. Dissect the shark, recover six embryos, and immediately introduce each embryo into the prepared artificial uterus. Visually assess embryos twice daily at 09:00 and 17:00 for respiratory behavior and light‑stimulus response. Maintain incubation fluid temperature at 12 °C throughout.

substeps.instruction: Capture pregnant shark at ~500 m depth.
Store fish in cooler box with seawater during transport.
Dissect fish and recover embryos.
Place each embryo into its incubation container immediately.
Observe embryos at 09:00 and 17:00 for gill‑flap movement, spiracular valve, body undulation, and posture changes.
Keep fluid temperature constant at 12 °C.

steps.title: Prepare artificial uterine fluid
steps.instruction: Dissolve 3.5 kg urea in 46 L chlorine‑free tap water, then add filtered seawater to bring the total volume to 100 L, yielding the artificial uterine fluid used for incubation.

substeps.instruction: Measure 3.5 kg urea.
Dissolve urea in 46 L chlorine‑free tap water.
Add filtered seawater until the solution reaches 100 L total volume.

steps.title: Acclimate embryos via stepwise mixing
steps.instruction: Gradually shift the incubation fluid composition toward full‑strength seawater by mixing artificial uterine fluid with seawater in the following ratios, each maintained for approximately one week: 100/0, 75/25, 50/50, 25/75, 12.5/87.5, and 6.3/93.7 (artificial uterine fluid : seawater).

substeps.instruction: Week 1: Use 100 % artificial uterine fluid, 0 % seawater.
Week 2: Mix 75 % artificial uterine fluid with 25 % seawater.
Week 3: Mix 50 % artificial uterine fluid with 50 % seawater.
Week 4: Mix 25 % artificial uterine fluid with 75 % seawater.
Week 5: Mix 12.5 % artificial uterine fluid with 87.5 % seawater.
Week 6: Mix 6.3 % artificial uterine fluid with 93.7 % seawater.

steps.title: Monitor fluid chemistry and replace fluid
steps.instruction: Every 2–4 days, measure sodium and urea; daily, measure ammonia using a DRI‑CHEM NX600 analyzer. When ammonia exceeds 200 µg/dL, replace the incubation fluid as follows: move the embryo to a clean container with fresh fluid, add 2 L fresh fluid to wash the embryo’s surface, place the container into a clean 8‑L aquarium filled with fresh fluid, and return it to the refrigerator. Wash the used aquarium and container with 0.1 % sodium hypochlorite, rinse with tap water, dry, and reuse for the next replacement.

substeps.instruction: Measure Na⁺ and urea every 2–4 days; measure NH₃ daily with DRI‑CHEM NX600.
If NH₃ > 200 µg/dL, perform fluid replacement:
a) Transfer embryo to a clean container containing fresh incubation fluid.
b) Pour an additional 2 L fresh fluid into the container to wash the embryo’s body surface.
c) Place the container (with embryo) into a clean 8‑L aquarium filled with fresh fluid.
d) Return the aquarium to the refrigerator.
e) Clean the used aquarium and container with 0.1 % sodium hypochlorite, rinse with tap water, dry, and set aside for reuse.
